p:
I'm— no, no, you're not. I'm saying that ICE is seeking detainer requests for people for a civil immigration enforcement matter. These individuals have come into contact with the state criminal justice system, right, or city agencies. So they're not— the federal government's not per se enforcing a criminal matter, but they have an opportunity to engage with our law enforcement entities and take these folks into custody and then engage in immigration enforcement. And those folks

have— can have their day in immigration court as to whether or not they should be removed or not. What is the virtue in the city shielding these people from that eventuality?

That is ultimately a policy discussion for the council. That is a— that is a balancing– the Council will set the— will set, and the administration will set the parameters of what city law will be. The Council and the city have set forth the laws as they are, and that's the law of the land, whether— certainly we could debate, you know, the virtue of one versus the other. We are looking at city law as it applies, or as the NYPD and the DOC complied with existing city law. We did not look at potential– anything relating to what the— respectfully, what the council member—

[interposing] Yeah, no, I respect that you're not a policymaker in this particular instance, but you know, you ventured forth a benefit of the process or of the sanctuary city policy in another matter, and you're straining to come up with one now because frankly there isn't one. And these folks who come into contact with the

criminal justice system should be handed over to ICE. And the legality of this local law that you're giving your report on is being litigated currently. The Department of Justice has sued the city in order to enforce the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution, rightly in my view. And so I think that, you know, the situations that New Yorkers are rightly concerned. And again, I'm not talking about the situations that you referenced earlier where folks, you know, may be going to school or engaging in city services or— when I'm talking about the people who come into contact with the criminal justice system because they've been arrested for crimes. And there's absolutely no earthly reason, good earthly reason, why the City of New York should be resisting federal detainer requests in those situations for civil immigration enforcement, right? So that's the point I'm making today, Commissioner. And unfortunately, I agree that you're not going to be the one to give give us the answer. The federal courts are going to do that hopefully soon. Thank you, Chairs.

Thank you, Council Member Carr. Before turning over to Council Member

Brewer, just a couple quick questions. Isn't it the law in this city that New York City agencies are not to assist federal— with federal immigration enforcement, barring limited circumstances?
Correct.
And isn't your role as the agency to ensure that the law is being followed?
That's correct.
And isn't it also a matter of separation opowers between local and federal government, that it is the responsibility of the federal government to carry out civil immigration enforcement?
That's correct.
And it is the responsibility of city government to carry out everyday city functions and services, correct?
That's right.

And in those instances where there may be sharing of information between the city and federal government, the sanctuary laws that we in the city have passed years

ago define explicitly those limited public safety circumstances, but they do exist, but limited public safety circumstances where such cooperation will be permissible. Isn't that correct [inaudible]
Yes, absolutely, there are. There are areas delineated in the law– to many ways to just to provide for the cooperation should it be necessary. Yes, that is in the law that's written.

And isn't it also correct that your report, DOI's report, identified instances where those laws were violated? In other words, where instances outside of those limited public safety circumstances, information was impermissibly shared between city and federal agencies. Isn't that right?
Yes, we saw that in the— that is detailed in the report.

And so isn't it also true that that raises a serious concern and risk that DOI also highlighted, that that when the law is not being followed, even with these limited exceptions, there are instances that have occurred

where outside of those exceptions, information has been impermissibly shared. Isn't it true that it also raises a concern for DOI in your report that there may be additional instances? There could be additional instances where such information was impermissibly shared outside of those exceptions, and your role is to ensure that that does not happen. Is that correct?

Yes, the recommendations we made relating to the audits were to capture exactly that, to determine whether or not there are any other instances that can be deterred, that can be identified in the past based on that type of audit. Yes.
Thank you. On that, oh– Chair Brooks-Powers also had one more question that she wanted to ask as well.

Commissioner, you also said a structure for an NYPD task force audit is under discussion. It's more than four months after your report came out and about a year since most events described in the reports. Do you consider

that kind of delay— do you consider that kind of delay the NYPD accepting DOI's recommendation?

Yes, my understanding is that the NYPD has been preparing and coming up with a methodology for doing that work, and I think, like, as I testified earlier, I think new– that this will all– this work will also dovetail with the new audits that the mayor has ordered happen at all six agencies. NYPD will be one of them. So any– whatever preparatory work they've already done for the audit will be included in the work that the mayor has detailed should be done, I think, under Senior Advisor Mostofi’s office.
And at what point do you consider delays a practical rejection, if at all?

I guess it's kind of a you know it when you see it situation. I don't think– I don't think we are– I don't think that's even close to being the case. And even– and a lot of the preparatory work that the NYPD– for an NYPD audit had already been underway even I think at the time that DOI issued its report. There's a—

there's an understanding of the work that needs to be done, and I believe there it's being done diligently and in good faith. I don't think there's any foot-dragging or delays at all. Certainly not the DOI has seen either in any of our conversations with
Thank you.
Thank you so much, Chair. Now turn over to Council Member Brewer.
Thank you. I think two things could be true. We can love David Carr and sanctuary city at the same time. So I just want to point that out.
Agreed.

Question is– first of all, congratulations also on your NYCHA report, which you just issued. Congratulations. With the issue of contracts, now that's not necessarily something that you looked at, but I'm interested, and I think the Chair is also, the role of private contracts in all of this, because obviously ICE probably works with companies. I know, for instance, there are ICE rentals in our city. Those are with

companies. So I just was wondering In the investigation, although I didn't see it here, was there any situation where you found contracts, city contracts, ICE contracts, in any way, shape, or form playing a role either through the audits, your investigation, and so on?
There was not, no.

Okay. Second question is, I think maybe you discussed this a little bit, to the— we're talking about Correction and NYPD. Any other agencies that have come to light in this investigation working with ICE?
No, these were very tailored to those two agencies, both based on the report– the refer— the referral from your office–
[interposing] Yep.
and from the former Speaker and from a DOC complaint. We did not look at any other agencies.

Okay. And so I know we talked about the audits quite a bit. So what is— but with both agencies, again, We don't know the

timeline, that's what you said, but is there— what do you hope to get out of the audits? What do you think they should be included, et cetera?

I mean, I think both audits were intended to be a review, a retrospective review, to see if there's any evidence as of what the Chairperson had, like, alluded to earlier. Could there be other instances that simply no one has uncovered yet? And I think the first– one of the ways that DOI thought would be an effective approach to that would be to look at email, for instance, in the NYPD context, within the communications between task force members to see if there were any requests being made, or anyone in the NYPD had received either an email request or a reference in email requests from the federal government that they were either concerned about or that were improper. I think that was a kind of a first step that would be a very discernible way of approaching, you know, that type of investigation, whether or not there's any email traffic relating to investigations.
And Corrections, same thing, or—
[interposing] Corrections–
[interposing] same idea?

Corrections, same, the same thing. I think the Corrections audit, um– we didn't necessarily mandate how the audit was to be affected. I think the NYPD focused on the email of task force officers as its first phase. I don't think the– I don't believe that DOC has concluded exactly what the focus of the audit will be, and I'm not quite sure what the new audit as mandated by the mayor, exactly how that's being structured, whether that's similar or broader, narrower. We hope to learn more about that once that begins to get up and running, and hopefully DOI can be an effective partner.

So how— I mean, when I'm on the street, the officers– PD I'm mostly with– they know for sure, do not coordinate with ICE. I got that. These federal task forces have existed

for a long time because you have to collaborate, coordinate, blah, blah, blah. So how do they operate? I mean, this is a different time. How do they operate now? How are they the– far as you know, similarly to how they in the past? Obviously there's a different president, for lack of a better word, who is conducting this— I consider them raids. Do they operate differently to the best of your knowledge, similarly? I mean, when you're talking to your friend who's an ICE employee and you're a PD, you know, you have to keep your distance, but you still have to coordinate, I guess, for safety of the country. So I don't know how– how do you think— is it different? Does it work similarly? Do you have any recommendations how these task forces should work? I know it's not necessarily PD to do this, but I just didn't know if you had any suggestions.
Well, I mean, obviously not part of the reports that the DOI issued.
Right.

My understanding generally is that the task forces that,

as you said, have been in place— Joint Terrorism Task Force, Joint Robbery Task Force— have been around forever.
Yep.

The hope is that the, you know, the purpose that is in the name of the task force, or HSI's Violent Crime Task Force, that they are true to the name of the task force and don't stray from that mission to keep the country safe from all sorts of different— from different topics that they were established for. I think the concern is, are they— are they doing that? But the structure, the structure is the same, and I can say that the NYPD has put in place safeguards to ensure that their officers and detectives are not being asked to do— to engage in practices that would be in violation of any city sanctuary city law. And those safeguards were both very intelligently designed and seem to be implemented well.

Okay. Just one last question. Ongoing, because this is obviously not ending in terms of the concern. So, I assume the audits will bring up whatever they bring up. But do

you have some suggestions as to ongoing? Maybe it's the mayor's executive order. What is it they can make sure that what you provided, what you found gets, A, addressed, but, B, doesn't happen again in the future? Is it more audits? Is it more— in my opinion, people don't have a clue what sanctuary city means. That's relevant. But any suggestions along those lines? How do we maintain the recommendations that you made and others that probably will maybe be discovered in the audits?

I think we'll know— I think we'll know more about that after the results of the audits. As I— as in my response to the Chairperson, you know, we don't know what we don't know. Hopefully the audits will fill in any gaps in our collective knowledge about what is happening right now, and I think that will be depending on what is uncovered, if anything, in the audit, I think will give us a better sense of the intensity or severity of the problem and whether or not, you know, if we see the– if we see, you know, a problem persisting and then since, you know, DOI's reports have been issued, the agency's taking corrective action. If we

kind of see, you know, some change in practice or change in frequency. I mean, I'm just— I'm kind of speculating.
Right.
But I think we'll know more once we see the audits and can see if we can see the patterns going in the right direction. I think that would be a good sign.

Okay. I mean, one of the issues is that they lie. I mean, the situation at Columbia with lying about a child in the dorm was challenging. So, I mean, I don't— you know, if the cops are told X is a child there and it could be something that they need to be involved in because it is relevant to them, but you're getting false information from ICE, it makes it hard to blame the cops for that. But so that's an example of just the worst of the worst. I obviously— hopefully that doesn't happen all the time.
Thank you. I'd like to acknowledge that we've also been joined by Council Member Narcisse. And next we have Council Member Zhuang.

Thank you, Chair. Thank you, Commissioner, to be here. I have a question. Probably a lot of people in the public are curious about this situation also. The Canal Street raid last year in November, NYPD and ICE showed up at the same time, and a lot of reporters, actually journalists, confirmed to my team that they got tipped off by NYPD about the Canal Street raid. Is that any coordination between NYPD and ICE in that situation? Did you guys do any investigation about that situation?
That was not the subject of our investigation. We did not look into– we did not look into that incident.
Okay, that's my question.
Thank you, Council Member Zhuang.
Thank you.

Oh, sorry, did you have more? No? Oh, thank you. And we've been joined by Council Member Narcisse, which was probably already said. I just have a few more questions, then

we turn it over to Department of Corrections for their testimony. Council Member Brewer and Chair Brooks-Powers also hit this point too. But Local Law 228 of 2017 prohibits the use of city property for immigration enforcement, and there are concerning instances where that might be happening or is happening. The Hudson River Park Trust— this has been reported in the news too— operates on city-owned land. Has the DOI considered investigating whether their contracts allowing ICE use of the piers violates the spirit or the letter of the city's sanctuary protections?
We are aware of that situation, and it is something that if DOI has the jurisdiction to review, we will do so. We are aware of it, and we're considering what our proper role in that would be.

Thank you. And I understand that the Hudson River Park Trust is a state city authority, but I do think the city's piers are city resources and land, and that would be something I would hope the DOI would be considering. And I should also add that we are hearing my

legislation soon in the Immigration Committee about prohibiting the city from contracting with ICE, because there are clearly gaps that are coming up that I'm— we're seeing very clearly need to be closed, especially at this moment. I wanted to go back to the joint task forces subject, and I bring that up because one thing that became clear from the DOI reports too is– and especially now, the way in which there are certainly, you know, state— sorry, city, federal task forces around criminal enforcement. But there's a real concern that those task forces, as we saw in these instances too, can bleed into impermissible information sharing around immigration enforcement. Instances where, for example, individuals were turned over impermissibly after they pled to misdemeanors even though they were originally char— and they were not pleading to or convicted of any of the serious felonies or otherwise that would qualify for information sharing. So there's a real question of how to ensure that criminal enforcement and cooperation there does not turn into something that it should not be turning into. You know, one question, and we've reviewed, you

know, at length DOC and what needs to happen there. But with NYPD task forces, do you all have a sense of how many NYPD officers are currently assigned to federal task forces that involve agencies that also have immigration enforcement authority?
I don't have that number. That is certainly something we could get back to the council with or– you refer to the NYPD as well.

If you do have that information, it'd be helpful. Otherwise, you can track it from NYPD as well. And do you all know, has NYPD conducted any internal reviews following your report about task force assignment, the risk assessment there, and what safeguards to put in place so there is no inadvertent facilitation of civil immigration enforcement?

Yes, certainly the NYPD could give you a better understanding of the– with exactly what they're doing. But our understanding from our– is that the NYPD has put in a series of controls elevating requests for information from the NYPD, elevating it from the task force

officer up to a supervisor. So before any information is shared between a federal— potentially federal immigration authority and the NYPD, there is a conversation between a NYPD supervisor with the supervisor from the federal authority, asking— as far as we can tell– the right questions to kind of— as opposed to task force officer and task force officer from different agencies, that is both— the NYPD has proactively elevated that up to a supervisory level, which is a very, you know, intelligent and well-considered risk management measures. Obviously, they’re trying to manage the risk and reduce the risk, but elevating it up to that management level is a— seems like a very— seemingly very intelligent control to put in place.

And on the topic of agency reporting requirements, is your— is it your interpretation that Local Law 228 of 2017, that NYPD, DOC, DOP, are required to report the same information as every other city agency on an annual basis, above and beyond the reporting required in the detainer laws? Would you agree that they're all subject to the same reporting requirements?

So my understanding is that the— as the law is written, there is no explicit exception for any of those agencies. So, they are without— without such an ex— without such an exception, they are– the law is applicable to them as any other agency. There doesn't seem to be anything special about that.
Have those agencies agreed with this interpretation or sent you notice that they agree as they've adopted the policy and procedure recommendations?
I don't believe we've had those conversations. That would be— we'd have to refer that back to the agencies.
Sure. Well, that concludes our questioning for you. Thank you, Commissioner. Oh, sorry, Council Member Narcisse has questions. Thank you. Almost done.
Very quickly. I'm not going to take you long.
Of course.

Knowing the City of New York, how complex that we are, right? We

want our community to be safe. We want the immigrants to be safe. And we need for— I mean, fair treatment. How your agency balance those priority in practice, those priorities in practice?

I mean, as the city's Inspector General, DOI provides oversight over, you know, the agencies on a variety of different matters. We take referrals very seriously, whether they're complaints from communities and in our outreach efforts, or, you know, or through the council as your constituents raise issues to you. But I think the man— the way we manage our oversight responsibilities across the city, across all all the agencies, we try to find, you know, that proper role of working with the agencies to make their service delivery better, to examine how they're engaging with their communities, and to make sure that everything is done in a professional, fair way that avoids risks of corruption and fraud and abuse. So we are certainly supportive of all the city agencies, and at the same time, we provide meaningful oversight. If we see any issues beginning to brew, we try to provide, you know, the kind of guidance and– to the city

agencies to get them, you know, through our policy and procedure recommendations to get them effectively working for their constituents. I don't know if that answers your—

Sort of. I know that my colleague, Gale Brewer, probably talk about the agency, how many— do you have enough staff to actually do the work? As a matter of that, one of the biggest supporters you have in here, always talking about the importance of giving you the support that you need, I mean, to do your job. So, sanctuary city always are very confusing things for a lot of people. From your perspective, can you describe it from your understanding? What is there and what is specific that you do?
What what we do–
[interposing] No, for sanctuary cities.
Oh. So, sure. So–
[interposing] Sorry, I apologize.

When we refer to sanctuary cities, we're talking about a series of, of City Council laws and mayoral orders that govern the manner in which city agencies are able to interact with federal immigration authorities and limit the city's ability to participate in any activities that would be considered prohibited activities relating to crimin— to civil immigration enforcement. It's a body of laws that govern this entire area, and we periodically see, you know, new laws added and new mayoral executive orders added, but it is that body of law that safeguards communities and allows people whose document— whose, immigration status may be either in flux or otherwise from, you know, enjoying the life here in New York that we all want to, you know, enjoy without the fear of you know, an interaction with a city— a necessary city agency causing them to be impacted with their— with federal immigration enforcement.
That's where things collide for us right now. So I'll yield back to my Chair. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you so much, Council Member Narcisse. Thank you, Commissioner. Appreciate all your great work–
[interposing] Thank you.
and your testimony today, too.
Thank you. I appreciate it.
Thank you. Now we'll be calling up representatives from the Department of Corrections to testify, and I'd ask the committee counsel to swear them in once they are seated.

Thank you, Chair Krishnan. We will now hear testimony from the New York City Department of Correction, specifically James Conroy. Before we begin, I will administer the affirmation. Panelists, please raise your right hand— Mr. Conroy, do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to councilmember questions?
I do.
Thank you. You may begin when ready.

Good morning, Chair Brooks-Powers and Chair Krishnan and members of the Committees on Criminal Justice and Oversight and Investigations. My name is James Conroy, and I'm the Deputy Commissioner of Legal Matters and General Counsel for the New York City Department of Correction. I appreciate the opportunity to testify today regarding the department's policies governing interactions with federal immigration authorities, the findings of the recent Department of Investigation report concerning DOC interactions with federal immigration authorities, and the steps the department has taken in response to DOI's findings and recommendations. The department has largely accepted DOI's recommendations and will detail how they have been implemented to-date to safeguard against an incident of this nature occurring again. This is the issue— this issue is one of importance to Commissioner Richards, and our goal today is to be clear and

transparent around our process and the steps we have and are taking to address this matter. The department's longstanding policies regarding interactions with federal immigration officials are grounded in New York City sanctuary city laws. In accordance with these laws, the department does not engage in immigration enforcement and does not subject its officers or employees to the direction of federal immigration enforcement authorities. As a matter of policy, the department does not honor Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainers absent a judicial warrant. In accordance with local law, if the department receives a detainer from ICE, in some circumstances ICE will be notified of an individual's discharge, but only if the individual in custody has a qualifying conviction as defined in local laws, meaning a conviction for a violent or otherwise serious crime within the past five years, or is identified as a possible match on a federal terrorist screening database. The request also must be supported by documentation establishing probable cause that the individual is subject to removal proceedings. This notification can be made in advance

of or when the discharge process begins. Importantly, the Department will not detain an individual beyond the time that the individual is authorized to be released from custody. Perhaps most significantly, if any of the required criteria are not met— meaning no qualifying conviction or no match in a terrorist screening database— DOC will not communicate with ICE about the individual in question. The Department's public reporting for the fiscal year reflects that cooperation under these in narrow circumstances is infrequent relative to the number of detainers that are lodged. Between July 2024 and June 2025, federal immigration authorities lodged 595 detainers and 19 individuals were transferred to federal authorities. This may be better illustrated through our calendar year statistics, however. In calendar year 2024, the Department recorded 403 detainer requests. Of those, there were 18 transfers. In the calendar year 2025, the Department recorded 895 detainer requests, and of those, 25 individuals were transferred. In September 2025, DOI issued a report that examined conduct by an investigator in the Correction Intelligence Bureau who was assigned to a joint federal task force. DOI

found that in two instances, the investigator inadvertently provided information about individuals in custody to federal immigration authorities in furtherance of civil immigration enforcement, despite that no detainer meeting the statutory criteria had been presented in connection with the individual. DOI further concluded that this assistance violated city law and DOC policy. In its findings, DOI found that the investigator did not understand that the assistance was being used for civil immigration enforcement rather than a federal criminal investigation, and that the Department had not provided sufficient training, guidance, or oversight to ensure that staff, particularly those assigned to federal task forces, could reliably distinguish between permissible coordination and impermissible civil immigration assistance. While DOI found that the investigator did not intend to violate the law and did not appreciate that the assistance was being used for civil immigration purposes, the fact remains that city resources were used in a manner that is inconsistent with the local laws. The conduct described in the report, although inadvertent, should

not have happened. The sanctuary city laws are clear, and the Department is bound and complies with them. We agree that clear guidance and robust training are necessary to ensure that these types of incidents do not occur again in the future. DOI issued several recommendations to prevent this type of incident from recurring. Recommendations include that DOC provide updated guidance and in-person training on applicable city law and department policy, clarify and streamline internal procedures regarding communication with federal partners, and assess whether any other instances of unauthorized assistance occurred, among other things. The Department has accepted the core recommendation and has already taken concrete steps to implement them. The first three recommendations made within the report relate to providing updated guidance and training on city law and policies and specific guidance on how to respond to requests from law enforcement partners and immigration-related requests. In response to those recommendations, the department's legal division conducted in-person training for relevant units that are most likely to

have contact with federal law enforcement partners. Training was conducted in April and May of 2025. The training reiterated obligations under local law and DOC policy, as well as proper communication protocols with federal immigration authorities. Additionally, since that time, the Legal Division has provided a training on this topic at each of the Department's leadership training courses for newly promoted captains and assistant deputy wardens. DOC is continuing to explore opportunities to expand training to additional personnel. In addition to the trainings, an agency-wide teletype was issued which was read to personnel over 21 consecutive roll calls, reiterating the internal policies regarding interactions with federal immigration authorities remain full and effective and must be strictly followed, and that any immigration-related requests must immediately be referred to the DOC ICE Unit and the DOC Legal Division. DOI also recommended that senior DOC officials coordinate with senior federal agency officials about limitations set forth in the city laws. DOC leadership has already met with senior officials and other agency liaisons at federal

agencies with whom its staff regularly collaborate. DOC will continue to engage federal agency partners on these issues and reiterate its commitment to ensure practices comply with all applicable laws and policy. As recommended, DOC also reported previously unknown interactions with appropriate city partners for public reporting purposes. Finally, DOI recommended certain policy changes as well as an agency-wide audit. While DOC has partially accepted these recommendations at the time of the report's publication, the Department is currently working to implement Mayoral Executive Order 13, which requires an audit and review of all agency policies and practices as it relates to interactions with federal immigration authorities. The work is underway, and the outcome of this collaborative assessment will guide future policy and training, which will be made publicly available on the department's website. The Department of Corrections is committed to the goals of upholding public safety and protecting the safety and security of all individuals in custody, as well as those working within the city jails. To be clear, those goals do not include enforcement of immigration

laws or in any way engaging in conduct that is inconsistent with this city's sanctuary city laws. We are grateful that these incidents were reported to help us ensure that we are addressing any gaps in the implementation of our policies, and we remain committed to the implementation of these laws and open to hearing from families, lawyers, elected officials, and others about issues and challenges as they arise. Thank you. I will— available to take questions. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Deputy Commissioner, for your testimony, and for appearing before us today. I have a few questions, and I'm going to turn it over to my co-chair, and then I'll come back and ask more after my colleagues ask questions, too. I appreciate your testimony today because, yeah, I think we are at a very crucial and concerning moment now. One of the themes that we keep hearing from advocates, and we're seeing in the Council is that this is not a new issue with DOC as well. There have been instances in the past, in the recent past, those reported, those likely not reported too, and I think, you know, what is new now

is a mayoral administration and leadership at DOC that is committed and shares our vision of addressing these issues. So we have this conflict here between what's happened in the past repeatedly without seeing change despite our hearings, but new leadership that shares our vision. And what I'd like to do in a constructive way is see how we can once and for all address these issues so that what happened under the prior mayoral administration, we break from that past and it does not happen again. But we make concrete efforts to do so. So on that note, can you just restate again— you did so in your testimony, but with new leadership, with Commissioner Richards there, with Mayor Mamdani and the new executive order as well— can you just restate how has the new leadership at DOC changed the agency's perspective about sanctuary law compliance?

Thank you. You know, as you know, Commissioner Richards is only in place for a few weeks now. And as you also know, the Department of Correction has a lot of things that we have on our plate and have to address. This is one of them. Um, obviously with Executive Order Number

13, it required us, and we have already begun to engage with City Hall and the Interagency Response Committee– if I misstated the name of that— but with the committee to begin the steps to enter into this audit and figure out how to do that more robustly. Commissioner Richard is clear that his vested interest in this agency, in collaboration with our city partners, is in accountability and transparency. And that is his mission statement, you know, to everyone in the department and to you know, city partners, and including the council. So that is what we are going to be doing and working towards. And again, we've already begun the work of conducting this audit to be in compliance not only with the, you know, emergency order— excuse me, Executive Order 13— but also just to look at our current policies and practices, as both the Department of Correction and City Hall will be doing, to see how it informs, uh, adjustments.

And, you know, I'm glad to hear that because I do think, as we saw and you probably heard with that prior question with DOI as well, these instances are likely not– we know not

isolated instances because there was a pervasive lack of training within DOC. And, you know, officers that are part of, you know, these larger efforts that are communicating unbeknownst to supervisors, you know, in violation of the law. They may not know the law themselves. You know, it's just what we see from all of the DOI investigation, which was not that long ago, it was just in the fall, was that these are systemic issues within the agency. And so, and again, that DOI report came out in September of 2025. So, you know, DOC is a very big agency, knowing government well, these things take time. So I suspect that these issues are still present as they were back in September and they will be now too for for you all to address. Uh, my question is, given the recent executive order, is it your testimony today that DOC will accept in full recommendation number six, requiring the agency from DOI to conduct a department-wide audit? Because one thing that really stood out to me, it was very concerning, was the prior administration's leadership at DOC refusing to accept that audit. And it seems to me that is the crux of what we're getting at here. So is it your

testimony today that DOC under this new administration will accept recommendation number six in conducting a department-wide audit?

If I may just first, Chair, clarify our acceptance or, position on that. The issue with the acceptance of that specific recommendation of a Department-wide audit was not that we are unwilling. What it really comes down to is the practicality of how our agency operates and functions. The reality for us is that agency-wide, the vast, vast majority of our officers up until very recently did not even have an email address, a department email address. When they are on post and on staff, they do not have access to computers or phones. So when we contemplated how and what we can do to do a department-wide audit, we thought most practically it would be, the most productive also to focus on the areas in which there is, and we know to be, this interaction. The reality is in our facilities, federal officials from any agency do not have direct access to just come onto Rikers Island and go to a facility so that you'd have, you know, direct interactions with the line

officers, you know, and there's a lot of different protocols and approvals that have to allow anyone to come onto Rikers Island. So, our not full acceptance of that is not, again, as an unwillingness. It was more we don't want to overpromise and underperform in that area. So that's, that's the nature of our response to that.
